claim: The hippocampus is a complex structure critically involved in numerous behavior-regulating systems.
source: The hippocampus is a complex structure critically involved in numerous behavior-regulating systems.
evidence: This is a general statement about hippocampal function that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: In young adults, multiple overlapping spatial modes along the hippocampus's longitudinal and transverse axes describe the organization of its functional integration with neocortex.
source: In young adults, multiple overlapping spatial modes along its longitudinal and transverse axes describe the organization of its functional integration with neocortex, extending the traditional framework emphasizing functional differences between sharply segregated hippocampal subregions.
evidence: This statement references established findings in the literature about hippocampal organization in young adults.

claim: The principal anteroposterior and second-order, mid-to-anterior/posterior hippocampal modes of neocortical functional connectivity represent distinct dimensions of macroscale cortical organization and manifest across the adult lifespan.
source: In two independent samples, we demonstrate that the principal anteroposterior and second-order, mid-to-anterior/posterior hippocampal modes of neocortical functional connectivity, representing distinct dimensions of macroscale cortical organization, manifest across the adult lifespan.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data from two independent samples.

claim: Individual differences in topography of the second-order gradient predicted episodic memory.
source: Specifically, individual differences in topography of the second-order gradient predicted episodic memory and mirrored dopamine D1 receptor distribution, capturing shared functional and molecular organization.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The second-order gradient mirrored dopamine D1 receptor distribution.
source: Specifically, individual differences in topography of the second-order gradient predicted episodic memory and mirrored dopamine D1 receptor distribution, capturing shared functional and molecular organization.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by PET imaging data.

claim: Older age was associated with less distinct transitions along gradients (i.e. increased functional homogeneity).
source: Older age was associated with less distinct transitions along gradients (i.e. increased functional homogeneity).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data analysis across age groups.

claim: A youth-like gradient profile predicted preserved episodic memory in older adults.
source: Importantly, a youth-like gradient profile predicted preserved episodic memory – emphasizing age-related gradient dedifferentiation as a marker of cognitive decline.
evidence: This is a finding supported by data comparing older adult subgroups.

claim: Age-related gradient dedifferentiation is a marker of cognitive decline.
source: Importantly, a youth-like gradient profile predicted preserved episodic memory – emphasizing age-related gradient dedifferentiation as a marker of cognitive decline.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed relationship between gradient profiles and memory performance.

claim: The hippocampus plays a critical role in human behavior beyond its well-established involvement in memory and spatial navigation.
source: The hippocampus plays a critical role in human behavior beyond its well-established involvement in memory and spatial navigation (Laurita and Spreng, 2017; Moscovitch et al., 2016; Nadel and Peterson, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The hippocampus's broad involvement in cognition emerges through the combination of its intrinsic circuitry and its widespread neocortical connections.
source: Contemporary views hold that its broad involvement in cognition emerges through the combination of its intrinsic circuitry and its widespread neocortical connections – placing it at the interface of multiple behavioral systems (Moscovitch et al., 2016; Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Animal models emphasize the hippocampus transverse (mediolateral) and longitudinal (anteroposterior) axes in determining its functional organization.
source: Animal models (Amaral and Witter, 1989; Witter and Amaral, 2021), together with histological and functional descriptions in humans (Amunts et al., 2005; Libby et al., 2012; Plachti et al., 2019), emphasize the hippocampus transverse (mediolateral) and longitudinal (anteroposterior) axes in determining its functional organization, contribution to behavior (Grady, 2020; Poppenk et al., 2013), and vulnerability to neurological disease (Lladó et al., 2018; Small et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to animal model studies.

claim: Resting-state fMRI has successfully provided functional analogues of the hippocampus canonical internal circuitry and its anatomical connections with neocortical areas in humans.
source: In humans, functional analogues of the hippocampus canonical internal circuitry and its anatomical connections with neocortical areas have successfully been provided by resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) (Libby et al., 2012; Dalton et al., 2019), at a coarse scale confirming the anteroposterior differentiation in connectivity observed in the animal literature (Amaral and Witter, 1989; Aggleton, 2012; Strange et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous fMRI studies.

claim: The anteroposterior organizational dimension of the hippocampus emerges consistently across studies.
source: Despite the consistency by which this anteroposterior organizational dimension emerges (Genon et al., 2021), significant questions however remain regarding its spatial distribution across cortex and its contribution to behavior across the adult human lifespan.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Several studies primarily attribute integration with the DMN to the posterior hippocampus.
source: Several studies primarily attribute integration with the DMN to the posterior hippocampus (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012; Libby et al., 2012; Adnan et al., 2016; Poppenk and Moscovitch, 2011), consistent with its anatomical connections to midline posterior parietal areas (Aggleton, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Other sources emphasize the anterior hippocampus as driving connectivity with the DMN.
source: Other sources emphasize the anterior hippocampus as driving connectivity with the DMN (Blessing et al., 2016; Chase et al., 2015; Zhong et al., 2019), on the basis of its anatomical connections with ventromedial prefrontal areas (Aggleton, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Inconsistencies in understanding hippocampal functional specialization stem from overlooking multiple overlapping and complementary functional modes.
source: We propose that inconsistencies in part stem from overlooking multiple overlapping and complementary functional modes, not discernable through traditional parcellation-based approaches, which assume homogeneous function within distinct, pre-defined, portions of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on inference from the literature.

claim: Hippocampal neocortical connectivity is fundamentally multidimensional in young adults.
source: Accumulating evidence in young adults indicate that hippocampal neocortical connectivity is indeed fundamentally multidimensional – organized in several overlapping, but distinct, spatial modes (Genon et al., 2021; Vos de Wael et al., 2018; Przeździk et al., 2019; Katsumi et al., 2023; Tian et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Gradient-based observations describe a principal anteroposterior mode of neocortical connectivity and identify orthogonal modes of long-axis and transverse variation in connectivity.
source: Whereas such gradient-based observations describe a principal anteroposterior mode of neocortical connectivity, they also identify orthogonal modes of long-axis and transverse variation in connectivity (Vos de Wael et al., 2018; Przeździk et al., 2019; Katsumi et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hippocampal gradients appear to reflect well-known gradients of macroscale brain function.
source: Importantly, these hippocampal gradients appear to reflect well-known gradients of macroscale brain function (Katsumi et al., 2023), which express functional differentiation across distinct cortical hierarchies (Huntenburg et al., 2018; Margulies et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The principal anteroposterior gradient has been linked to functional differentiation along a task-negative/task-positive cortical dimension.
source: The principal anteroposterior gradient has been linked to functional differentiation along a task-negative/task-positive cortical dimension (Fox et al., 2005), separating neural communities involved in the formation of representations from sensory input (e.g. visual, somatosensory, and DMN areas) and those involved in the modulation of these representations (e.g. frontoparietal areas of attention and control) (Katsumi et al., 2023; Margulies et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A secondary, nonlinear, long-axis gradient is suggested to correspond to the principal unimodal-transmodal gradient of cortical function.
source: In parallel, a secondary, nonlinear, long-axis gradient is suggested to correspond to the principal unimodal-transmodal gradient of cortical function (oppositely anchored in associative DMN areas and in unimodal sensory and motor cortices [Huntenburg et al., 2018; Margulies et al., 2016; Katsumi et al., 2023]).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The biological underpinnings of the secondary gradient remain unknown.
source: However, the biological underpinnings of this secondary gradient remain still unknown, in contrast to the principal gradient, demonstrated also in microstructure (Adnan et al., 2016), gray matter covariance (Plachti et al., 2019; Ge et al., 2019), and gene expression (Vogel et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in knowledge while citing evidence for the principal gradient.

claim: Differences in the topography of the principal, anteroposterior, hippocampal gradient may predict episodic memory.
source: Differences in the topography (i.e. the spatial layout) of the principal, anteroposterior, hippocampal gradient may predict episodic memory (Przeździk et al., 2019), but current findings are restricted to younger age – and to mainly the same sample (i.e. the Human Connectome Project [Van Essen et al., 2013; Vos de Wael et al., 2018; Przeździk et al., 2019; Katsumi et al., 2023]).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Aging has been linked to differential functional isolation of anterior and posterior hippocampal regions from prefrontal areas and large-scale brain networks including the DMN.
source: Specifically, aging has been linked to differential functional isolation of anterior and posterior hippocampal regions from prefrontal areas and large-scale brain networks including the DMN (Damoiseaux et al., 2016; Salami et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neocortical disconnection of hippocampal subregions has been linked to dysfunction during memory encoding and retrieval.
source: Such neocortical disconnection of hippocampal subregions has been linked to dysfunction during memory encoding and retrieval (Salami et al., 2016; Nyberg et al., 2019; Salami et al., 2014), and, in turn, to episodic memory decline (Salami et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hippocampal isolation is driven by the spatial patterns in which Alzheimer's disease pathology accumulates in cognitively healthy older adults.
source: Findings which link hippocampal isolation to increased functional homogeneity within the region suggest that its disconnection from neocortex is driven by the spatial patterns in which Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology accumulates in cognitively healthy older adults (Berron et al., 2021; Harrison et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of functional segregation between task-negative and task-positive poles is a functional hallmark of both healthy aging and AD.
source: Importantly, loss of functional segregation between task-negative and task-positive poles is a functional hallmark of both healthy aging (Grady et al., 2016) and AD (Weiler et al., 2017) – introducing overall ambiguity as to whether hippocampal gradients established in young adults persist into older age.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Dopamine is one of the most important modulators of hippocampus-dependent function.
source: Dopamine (DA) is one of the most important modulators of hippocampus-dependent function (Edelmann and Lessmann, 2018; El-Ghundi et al., 2007) and influences the brain's functional architecture through enhancing specificity of neuronal signaling (Seamans and Yang, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is a DA-dependent aspect of maintained functional network segregation in aging which supports cognition.
source: Consistently, there is a DA-dependent aspect of maintained functional network segregation in aging which supports cognition (Pedersen et al., 2023b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Animal models suggest heterogeneous patterns of DA innervation and postsynaptic DA receptors across both transverse and longitudinal hippocampal axes.
source: Animal models suggest heterogeneous patterns of DA innervation (Gasbarri et al., 1994; Kempadoo et al., 2016) and postsynaptic DA receptors (Dubovyk and Manahan-Vaughan, 2019), across both transverse and longitudinal hippocampal axes, likely allowing for separation between DA modulation of distinct hippocampus-dependent behaviors (Edelmann and Lessmann, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to animal model studies.

claim: The human hippocampus has been linked to distinct DA circuits on the basis of long-axis variation in functional connectivity with midbrain and striatal regions.
source: Moreover, the human hippocampus has been linked to distinct DA circuits on the basis of long-axis variation in functional connectivity with midbrain and striatal regions (Kahn and Shohamy, 2013; Nordin et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The principal gradient (G1) explained 44% and 53% of the variance in left and right hemispheres, respectively.
source: The principal gradient (G1), explaining 44% and 53% of the variance in left and right hemispheres, was organized along the hippocampus longitudinal axis, conveying gradual anterior-to-posterior variation in cortical connectivity (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The second-order gradient (G2) explained 11% of the variance in both hemispheres.

evidence: This is a finding supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: G2 expressed a secondary long-axis gradient organized from the middle hippocampus toward anterior and posterior ends.

claim: The third-order gradient (G3) explained 8% and 7% of the variance in left and right hemispheres, respectively.
source: Finally, the third-order gradient (G3), explaining 8% and 7% of the variance, reflected variation along the hippocampus transverse axis, such that inferior-lateral parts of the hippocampus were separated from medial-superior parts (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CA1–3 expressed the full extent of the G3 gradient.
source: Inspecting G3 across sample-specific segmentations of cornu ammonis (CA1–3), dentate gyrus (DG/CA4), and subiculum subfields suggested that while CA1–3 expressed the full extent of the gradient, and DG/CA4 variation around its center, the subiculum expressed only the most inferior section of the gradient (Appendix 1—figure 2).

source: The three gradients reflected gradients identified in young adults (Vos de Wael et al., 2018; Przeździk et al., 2019; Katsumi et al., 2023) and were highly reproducible in the independent replication dataset (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding supported by replication analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: Areas of the DMN most strongly mapped onto the most inferior end of G3, consistent with the connectivity profile of the subiculum.

source: Moreover, we demonstrate in two independent samples that maintaining a youth-like gradient profile in older age – characterized by preserved distinctiveness of connectivity change along gradients – supports mnemonic functioning, and that increased homogeneity of gradient topography may precede gray matter atrophy.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on findings from two independent samples.

claim: Functional data favors detection of anteroposterior hippocampal organization in contrast to that determined by its cytoarchitecture.
source: Our results confirm that functional data favors detection of anteroposterior hippocampal organization in contrast to that determined by its cytoarchitecture (Genon et al., 2021), but indicate that higher-order connectivity modes may indeed carry coarse-scale information about subfield-determined organization.
evidence: This is an interpretation of results in light of previous literature.

claim: An account of the hippocampus functional connectivity with the DMN is dependent on multiple neurofunctional hierarchies.
source: Taken together, our observations support a framework of cortico-hippocampal integration in which the DMN is positioned in different neural contexts: in one case at the opposite end from frontoparietal networks of attention and control, and in the other, opposite to sensorimotor and visual networks – indicating that an account of the hippocampus functional connectivity with the DMN is dependent on multiple neurofunctional hierarchies.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed relationships between gradients and cortical networks.

source: Moreover, the observation that macroscale relationships between distinct cortical systems are mapped out by G1 and G2 in this manner may reflect the hippocampus primordial position in the laminar development of the cerebral cortex (Goulas et al., 2019), supporting the idea that hippocampal function stands, from a phylogenetic perspective, to inform general principles of brain organization (Genon et al., 2021).

claim: G2 may constitute a mode reflecting a dopaminergic phenotype.

evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed correspondence with multiple DA markers.
